title: Gold's Asian hours are priced by a physical bid that keeps a Chinese calendar: on days the Shanghai Gold Exchange is shut the largest quota-constrained buyer in the world is absent, and after a long closure it must restock

scout.mechanism: During the Asian session the marginal participant in gold is not a macro speculator; it is physical. The Shanghai Gold Exchange is the mandatory venue through which imported bullion enters China, and the banks that hold PBoC import quotas buy London metal and deliver it into Shanghai. That flow is forced twice over: the quota holder has customers (refiners, jewellers, the retail bar market) with delivery obligations, and the import channel is administratively licensed so the flow cannot be re-routed, re-timed or scaled at will. The SGE keeps the Chinese public-holiday calendar — a calendar set annually by State Council decree, which moves with the lunar new year, bolts single days onto adjacent weekends, and designates ordinary Saturdays as working days in compensation. It is not the calendar in anybody's terminal. Two consequences, both testable and both about a forcer rather than a pattern. (a) On a weekday when the SGE is closed and London and New York are open, the Asian-hours bid is missing and gold's Asian session should behave measurably differently from an ordinary weekday's — not merely quieter, but with its drift removed, because the absent participant is one-sided. (b) After a multi-day closure (Spring Festival, National Day), the quota holders reopen with several days of accumulated delivery obligations and must restock — a deadline-driven, one-directional burst concentrated into the first reopened Asian session. The second half is the stronger claim because it has a sign the first half does not.
scout.why_unarbitraged: The constraint is regulatory and cannot be arbitraged away — that is the brief's own example of a valid answer and it is literally true here: the import quota is an administrative licence issued by a central bank, so no amount of capital can supply the missing bid on a closed day or smooth the restocking burst across the closure. The residual survives being known for two further reasons. First, the calendar is genuinely awkward: it is published in Chinese, it changes every year by decree, it contains make-up working Saturdays that no Western holiday table models, and it must be pinned per year with provenance rather than generated by a rule — the same standard docs/news/README.md already applies to the Fed, BLS and ECB, and the same reason data/news/raw/bls-2027.txt sits on disk with zero rows. Second, the effect lives in Asian hours, which is the part of the day that a London or New York desk does not staff and does not want to carry risk in; the participants who WOULD arbitrage it are in the wrong time zone, and the ones in the right time zone are the quota holders themselves, who are the forced side. Honest weakness: gold is fungible and twenty-four-hour, so an absent Shanghai bid can in principle be replaced by London or Comex arbitrage within hours. If it is, this dies, and the falsifier is built to show that.
data_needed: data/bars/XAUDUKA-1m.parquet — ON DISK: 5,635,777 minutes, 2010-06-01 to 2026-05-31, twenty-four hours a day, flat zero-volume bars already dropped (docs/decisions/2026-09-13-night-synthesis.md, process change 7). Sixteen years gives roughly 350 to 450 SGE-closed weekdays and sixteen Spring Festival reopens plus sixteen National Day reopens — enough to split into two eight-year windows the way every record in this loop does.

data/bars/XAGDUKA-1m.parquet — ON DISK: silver, the natural second asset. Silver is also traded on the SGE and is also import-constrained, so the same test should fire there; if the effect is gold-only it is more likely a calendar artefact than a physical-flow one.

NOT ON DISK, and it is a data task not a research one: a China public-holiday and SGE trading calendar for 2010-2026, pinned per year with the source page and fetch date in a raw file, including make-up working Saturdays. Several maintained open datasets of State Council holiday decrees exist; the SGE also publishes its own annual trading-calendar notice. This must be assembled and reviewed before any return is read, exactly as data/news/events-extended.csv was assembled before the 08:30-release question could be asked.

NOT NEEDED, and this is deliberate: the SGE PRICE (the Shanghai premium over London) is NOT required and should not be used in the first pass. Assembling sixteen years of SGE Au99.99 benchmark prices and the CNY fix is a much harder data problem, and a premium-conditioned version of this idea should be a successor registration, not a prerequisite. The closure calendar alone is a clean instrument: it is exogenous to the gold price, decided by decree a year in advance.

Vantage costs from config/default.toml (XAUUSD.sc spread 0.28, swap 0.00). An Asian-session hold of a few hours, or one session held over the reopen, is priced at 0.28 an ounce; the spread probe of 2026-09-15 measured p50 0.19-0.20 through Asia, so the registration should say which number it charges and why.
scout.falsifier_sketch: Two arms, declared separately, and each can close on its own. ARM A (absence): the statistic is the median Asian-session return (00:00-07:00 UTC, clocked to the session and not to a bar count, per fault 12 in docs/decisions/2026-09-13-instrument-faults.md) on SGE-closed weekdays versus SGE-open weekdays. No direction is declared for Arm A — an absent bid removes a drift rather than reversing one — so Arm A's falsifier is a magnitude: it dies unless the difference in medians reaches the 95th percentile of a null that permutes the closed-day flag across weekdays MATCHED ON DAY OF WEEK AND MONTH, because Chinese holidays cluster in January, February and October and a month-blind null would be a seasonality null. ARM B (restock), which is the arm worth trading: after a closure of three or more consecutive SGE trading days, the declared direction is that the first reopened Asian session's return is POSITIVE, and no mirror is available. It dies if the sign rate is <= 50%, if it fails the 95th percentile of the same day-of-week-and-month-matched null at 100,000 draws (standard error 0.07 pp, per the standing precision item in BACKLOG.md), or if the sample is too small to resolve — with roughly thirty-two reopens in sixteen years the minimum detectable effect must be stated BEFORE the window is opened, and if it cannot reach the gate the verdict is 'underpowered', recorded as such, not 'no'. Two pre-declared placebos that close both arms regardless of percentile: (1) the same test on EURUSD (data/bars/EURDUKA-1m.parquet), which has no Chinese physical channel — if the euro's Asian session responds to the SGE calendar, the calendar is picking up a global holiday-liquidity effect and not a gold-specific bid; (2) the same test on days when the SGE is open but a Chinese holiday falls on a WEEKEND, where the decreed holiday exists but the missing-bid mechanism does not. Report the null's centre and a day-block bootstrap interval next to every percentile, per the standing rule from 2026-09-15-venue-residual.
scout.closest_known: docs/decisions/2026-09-14-nfp-vs-first-friday.md is the nearest relative and the reason this is worth proposing. That record closed because the desk's calendar had five event names and could not tell a quiet Friday from one carrying Canada's Labour Force Survey — the finding was that THE CALENDAR WAS THE THING THAT WAS WRONG, and the repair (data/news/events-extended.csv, 2026-09-15) extended it by exactly two Western releases. This proposal is the same lesson pushed one step further: the desk's calendar is still entirely North Atlantic, and the participant that actually clears physical gold in the hours before London opens keeps a different one. Second closest: docs/decisions/2026-09-13-btc-us-hours.md and 2026-09-14-fx-local-hours.md, the two records that tested a session's drift. Both are clock claims — hold these hours, every day, unconditionally — and both closed in the shape the night synthesis describes, worth about the spread and gone on the second window. This is not a clock claim: the hours are held only on days selected by an exogenous calendar, and the traded arm (Arm B) fires about twice a year on a deadline, which is a different object from a daily hold. If the historian reads Arm A as a session-drift variant it should be dropped and Arm B registered alone.
